title: Branch Prediction
summary: Why deep, wide pipelines demand highly accurate dynamic branch prediction, and the predictor structures that deliver it.

slides.markdown:
A control hazard ([control-hazards-and-branching](control-hazards-and-branching)) costs more the deeper and wider a pipeline gets: a misprediction flushes every in-flight instruction behind the branch, and modern cores keep far more instructions in flight than a classic 5-stage pipeline ever did.

A 20-stage, 6-wide OoO core can have well over 100 instructions in flight — a mispredicted branch flushes all of them, costing tens of cycles. That's why prediction accuracy, not just pipeline depth or issue width, is one of the biggest levers on real single-thread performance today.

Static schemes ([control-hazards-and-branching](control-hazards-and-branching)) — always-not-taken, always-taken, or backward-taken/forward-not-taken — guess the same way every time a given branch is seen, using no runtime history at all.

They work reasonably for a few common patterns (loop-closing backward branches are usually taken) but hit a hard ceiling around 60–70% accuracy on real code — nowhere near good enough when a misprediction flush costs tens of cycles on every one of the many branches typical code executes.

**Dynamic prediction** tracks each branch's runtime history in a **branch history table (BHT)**, indexed by the branch's address. The classic entry is a **2-bit saturating counter** with four states — strongly/weakly not-taken, weakly/strongly taken — that shifts one step toward the outcome it just saw.

The 2-bit design (versus a 1-bit flag) exists so **one atypical outcome inside a mostly-consistent loop doesn't flip the prediction** — the counter needs two wrong-direction outcomes in a row before it changes, which meaningfully improves accuracy on real loop patterns.

![A 2-bit saturating counter's four states transitioning across a sequence of taken and not-taken outcomes](assets/2bit-counter.svg)

Each outcome nudges the counter one state toward or away from "taken"; it only crosses the taken/not-taken boundary (and thus flips the actual prediction) after two consecutive outcomes disagree with the current strong state — one stray branch inside a 99%-taken loop barely dents accuracy.

assets.alt: A 2-bit saturating counter's four states transitioning across a sequence of taken and not-taken outcomes

slides.markdown:
A per-branch 2-bit counter ignores context: many branches correlate with *other* recent branches, not just their own past. **Correlating predictors** index using a **global history register** — the last N branch outcomes anywhere in the program — combined with the branch address, learning patterns like "this branch usually goes opposite the one two instructions ago."

This captures more real branch behavior than any single branch's history could — why most high-performance cores use global or hybrid schemes over plain per-branch counters.

Predicting *taken vs not-taken* is only half the job — for a taken branch, the front end also needs to know **where** to fetch from next, before the target address is even computed. The **branch target buffer (BTB)** is a small cache mapping a branch's address to the target it went to last time, letting fetch redirect immediately on a predicted-taken branch instead of waiting for the branch to actually execute.

Direction and target prediction are genuinely separate structures solving separate problems, and both have to be right for the fetch stream to stay on the correct path.

slides.sectionTitle: Predictor design and its blind spot
slides.markdown:
| Predictor | Accuracy | Hardware cost |
|---|---|---|
| Local (per-branch 2-bit) | Good | Small |
| Global/correlating | Better on branches with cross-branch patterns | Larger history register + table |
| Hybrid (tournament) | Best — picks whichever predictor is historically more accurate per branch | Highest — runs multiple predictors plus a selector |

**How to decide:** hybrid predictors dominate in high-performance cores where transistor budget allows it; simpler local predictors still suit area-constrained cores. **Pitfall:** even a perfectly predicted *direction* still costs performance if the BTB mispredicts the *target* — a correct "taken" guess with the wrong destination still triggers a full pipeline flush.
